records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלִישָׁ֔ע שִׁמְע֖וּ דְּבַר־יְהוָ֑ה כֹּ֣ה׀אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה כָּעֵ֤ת׀מָחָר֙ סְאָֽה־סֹ֣לֶת בְּשֶׁ֗קֶל וְסָאתַ֧יִם שְׂעֹרִ֛ים בְּשֶׁ֖קֶל בְּשַׁ֥עַר שֹׁמְרֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And said Elisha, Hear [the] word of Yahweh; thus says Yahweh: About [this] time tomorrow a seah of fine flour for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, in [the] gate of Samaria.
pieces: Elisha said, "Listen to the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: 'About this time tomorrow, {{units:about 7 quarts|a seah}} of fine flour will sell for {{units:about 2/5 ounce of silver|a shekel}}, and {{units:about 13 quarts|two seahs}} of barley for {{units:about 2/5 ounce of silver|a shekel}}, at the gate of Samaria.'"

L.1: And Elisha said, "Hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: 'About [this] time tomorrow a seah of fine flour [will sell] for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria.'"

R.1: Elisha answered, "Listen to the message from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: 'By this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, you will be able to buy {{units:about 7 quarts|a seah}} of the best flour for {{units:about 2/5 ounce of silver|a shekel}}. And you will be able to buy {{units:about 13 quarts|two seahs}} of barley for the same price.'"

decisions.choice: a seah: a dry measure, perhaps about 7 quarts; a shekel: a weight of silver
decisions.reason: A seah was a dry measure for grain and flour, a third of an ephah by later reckoning. Its exact size is not known; estimates run from about 6 to about 13 quarts, so the modern figure is only a guide. A shekel was a weight of silver, not a coin. The prices are low after the famine of 6:25, when a donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver.

decisions.choice: fine flour and barley: the best flour and the cheaper grain
decisions.reason: Fine flour was finely ground wheat flour, the kind used in offerings (Leviticus 2:1). Barley was the cheaper grain, so twice as much of it sells for the same price. Both prices together say that food will be plentiful again.

decisions.choice: about this time tomorrow: within a day
decisions.reason: The phrase sets a limit of one day (Genesis 18:10 uses a similar time phrase). Elisha answers the despair spoken in 6:33, where the king's messenger asks why he should wait for Yahweh any longer.

decisions.choice: the gate of Samaria: the city's market place
decisions.reason: The open space at a city gate was where people met, traded and held court (Genesis 23:10; Ruth 4:1). Food would be sold there, and the crowd there matters again in verse 17.

decisions.choice: about 7 quarts; about 13 quarts; about 2/5 ounce of silver
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give modern measures with the Hebrew units as the alternative, as earlier chapters give two seahs as about 13 quarts. Literal keeps seah and shekel.

decisions.choice: you will be able to buy ... for the same price
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that this is a price people will pay, and says "the same price" rather than repeating the weight of silver.

records.heading: Elisha promises food

records.source: וַיַּ֣עַן הַשָּׁלִ֡ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־לַמֶּלֶךְ֩ נִשְׁעָ֨ן עַל־יָד֜וֹ אֶת־אִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים֮ וַיֹּאמַר֒ הִנֵּ֣ה יְהוָ֗ה עֹשֶׂ֤ה אֲרֻבּוֹת֙ בַּשָּׁמַ֔יִם הֲיִהְיֶ֖ה הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הִנְּכָ֤ה רֹאֶה֙ בְּעֵינֶ֔יךָ וּמִשָּׁ֖ם לֹ֥א תֹאכֵֽל׃ס
records.gloss: And answered the officer who [was] to the king, leaning on his hand, the man of God and said, Look, Yahweh [is] making windows in the heavens; will be the thing this? And he said, Look, you [are] seeing with your eyes, but from there not you will eat.
pieces: The officer whose arm the king leaned on replied to the man of God, "Even if {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} were to make floodgates in the heavens, could this really happen?" Elisha replied, "With your own eyes you will see it happen, but you will not eat any of it."

L.2: And the officer on whose hand the king was leaning answered the man of God and said, "Look, [even if] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} were making windows in the heavens, could this thing happen?" And he said, "Look, you are going to see [it] with your own eyes, but you will not eat from it."

R.2: The king's personal officer, the man the king leaned on, said to the man of God, "Even if {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} opened windows in the sky, could this really happen?" Elisha answered, "You will see it happen with your own eyes. But you will not eat any of that food."

decisions.choice: the officer: a high-ranking officer close to the king
alternatives: the third man in a chariot
decisions.reason: The word is related to the word for "three". It may first have named the third man in a war chariot, beside the driver and the fighter, and it came to name a high-ranking officer (Exodus 14:7; 9:25; 10:25; 15:25). Here he is the king's personal aide.

decisions.choice: on whose hand the king leaned: the king's trusted attendant
decisions.reason: The king leaned on this man's arm when he walked or stood in public. It marks the man as his closest attendant, as Naaman's master leaned on Naaman's hand (5:18). The Hebrew word order is unusual ("who to the king, leaning on his hand"), but the sense is clear from verse 17.

decisions.choice: windows in the heavens: openings through which water pours from above
decisions.reason: At the flood "the windows of the heavens were opened" and rain poured down (Genesis 7:11; 8:2). Malachi 3:10 uses the picture for an overflowing blessing. The officer means that even rain from heaven could not bring food so quickly: crops take months to grow.

decisions.choice: look, if Yahweh made windows ...: a scornful "even if"
alternatives: Look, Yahweh is making windows in the heavens! Could this happen?
decisions.reason: The word "look" can introduce a supposed case ("suppose that"), and the question that follows expects the answer no. The officer does not doubt that Yahweh could open heaven; he doubts that anything at all could make Elisha's words come true.

decisions.choice: he said: Elisha answers the officer
decisions.reason: The speaker is not named, but it is the man of God, as verse 19 repeats. "You will see" uses the participle for something about to happen. The words come true in verse 17.

decisions.choice: floodgates
decisions.reason: Balanced says "floodgates" for these windows of rain, as at Genesis 7:11, so the link to the flood stays visible. Literal and Readable keep "windows".

decisions.choice: on whose arm; Elisha replied; the king's personal officer
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "arm" where the Hebrew says "hand", since that is what one leans on. They name Elisha as the speaker. Readable explains the officer's place beside the king.

records.source: וְאַרְבָּעָ֧ה אֲנָשִׁ֛ים הָי֥וּ מְצֹרָעִ֖ים פֶּ֣תַח הַשָּׁ֑עַר וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֔הוּ מָ֗ה אֲנַ֛חְנוּ יֹשְׁבִ֥ים פֹּ֖ה עַד־מָֽתְנוּ׃
records.gloss: And four men were with scale disease [at the] entrance of the gate; and said each to his neighbor, Why [are] we sitting here until we die?
pieces: Now there were four men with a serious skin disease at the entrance to the city gate. They said to one another, "Why are we sitting here waiting to die?"

L.3: Now four men with scale disease were at the entrance of the gate, and they said each to his companion, "Why are we sitting here until we die?"

R.3: Four men who had a serious skin disease were sitting just outside the city gate. They said to each other, "Why should we stay here until we die?"

decisions.choice: with scale disease: suffering from a skin disease that made a person unclean, not modern leprosy
decisions.reason: The word is the one used in Leviticus 13-14 for skin conditions with visible signs, such as swellings, scabs or white patches. Leprosy as known today (Hansen's disease) does not fit those signs well. The law treated it as uncleanness, and a person who had it lived outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46; Numbers 5:2-3).

decisions.choice: at the entrance of the gate: outside the city, but near it
decisions.reason: Being unclean, the four men could not live inside Samaria, so they stayed by the gate, where people coming and going might give them food. In a city under siege no food was coming out.

decisions.choice: why are we sitting here until we die?: a question that expects no answer
decisions.reason: The question means that staying where they are only leads to death. Verse 4 spells out their reasoning.

decisions.choice: scale disease; a serious skin disease
decisions.reason: These are the words used for the same Hebrew term in Leviticus 13 and Numbers 5:2: Literal "scale disease", Balanced and Readable "a serious skin disease". They avoid suggesting modern leprosy.

records.heading: Four men find the camp deserted

records.source: אִם־אָמַרְנוּ֩ נָב֨וֹא הָעִ֜יר וְהָרָעָ֤ב בָּעִיר֙ וָמַ֣תְנוּ שָׁ֔ם וְאִם־יָשַׁ֥בְנוּ פֹ֖ה וָמָ֑תְנוּ וְעַתָּ֗ה לְכוּ֙ וְנִפְּלָה֙ אֶל־מַחֲנֵ֣ה אֲרָ֔ם אִם־יְחַיֻּ֣נוּ נִֽחְיֶ֔ה וְאִם־יְמִיתֻ֖נוּ וָמָֽתְנוּ׃
records.gloss: If we say, We will enter the city, and the famine [is] in the city, and we will die there; and if we sit here, and we will die; and now come and let us fall to [the] camp of Aram; if they let us live, we will live, and if they put us to death, and we will die.
pieces: "If we say, 'Let us go into the city,' the famine is there, and we will die there. If we stay here, we will die. So come, let us go over to the Aramean camp and surrender. If they spare us, we will live; if they kill us, we will die."

L.4: "If we say, 'We will enter the city,' then the famine [is] in the city, and we will die there; and if we sit here, we will die. So now come, and let us fall away to the camp of Aram. If they let us live, we will live; and if they put us to death, we will die."

R.4: "If we decide to go into the city, we will die there, because there is no food in the city. But if we stay here, we will die too. So let us go to the camp of the Aramean army and give ourselves up. If they spare us, we will stay alive. And if they kill us, we die."

decisions.choice: fall to the camp: go over to the enemy and surrender
decisions.reason: To "fall to" an enemy means to desert to them and give oneself up (Jeremiah 21:9; 37:13-14; 38:19). The men plan to surrender to the Arameans in the hope of being fed.

decisions.choice: the camp of Aram: the Aramean army besieging Samaria
decisions.reason: Ben-hadad king of Aram had gathered his whole army and laid siege to Samaria (6:24). Aram, the kingdom whose capital was Damascus, is named here for its army.

decisions.choice: if we say: if we decide
decisions.reason: To "say" here is to make up one's mind, as often in Hebrew. The men weigh three choices: the city, staying where they are, and the enemy camp. Only the last gives them any hope.

decisions.choice: go over ... and surrender; give ourselves up; the Aramean camp
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable spell out what "fall to" the camp means (m1), and call Aram "the Arameans", as they do through the chapter.

decisions.choice: because there is no food in the city
decisions.reason: Readable explains what "the famine is in the city" means for the men.

records.source: וַיָּק֣וּמוּ בַנֶּ֔שֶׁף לָב֖וֹא אֶל־מַחֲנֵ֣ה אֲרָ֑ם וַיָּבֹ֗אוּ עַד־קְצֵה֙ מַחֲנֵ֣ה אֲרָ֔ם וְהִנֵּ֥ה אֵֽין־שָׁ֖ם אִֽישׁ׃
records.gloss: And they arose at twilight to go to [the] camp of Aram; and they came to [the] edge of [the] camp of Aram, and look, there was not there a man.
pieces: So at dusk they got up and set out for the Aramean camp. But when they reached the edge of the camp, there was no one there at all.

L.5: And they got up at twilight to go to the camp of Aram. And they came to the edge of the camp of Aram, and look, there was no one there.

R.5: When it was getting dark, they got up and went toward the Aramean camp. But when they came to the edge of the camp, no one was there!

decisions.choice: twilight: the dusk of evening
decisions.reason: The word can mean the dim light of evening or of early morning. Here it is evening: the men later wonder whether to wait "until the morning light" (verse 9). The Arameans fled at the same twilight (verse 7).

decisions.choice: the edge of the camp: its nearest part
decisions.reason: The edge is the outskirts of the camp, the part the men reached first, coming from the city.

decisions.choice: and look, there was no one there: the scene through the men's eyes
decisions.reason: The word "look" shows what the men suddenly saw. The surprise is told from their point of view before verse 6 explains it.

decisions.choice: But ... at all; no one was there!
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable carry the surprise of "look" with "but", "at all" or an exclamation, rather than an old-fashioned "behold".

records.source: וַאדֹנָ֞י הִשְׁמִ֣יעַ׀אֶת־מַחֲנֵ֣ה אֲרָ֗ם ק֥וֹל רֶ֨כֶב֙ ק֣וֹל ס֔וּס ק֖וֹל חַ֣יִל גָּד֑וֹל וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־אָחִ֗יו הִנֵּ֣ה שָֽׂכַר־עָלֵינוּ֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל אֶת־מַלְכֵ֧י הַחִתִּ֛ים וְאֶת־מַלְכֵ֥י מִצְרַ֖יִם לָב֥וֹא עָלֵֽינוּ׃
records.gloss: And [the] Lord had caused [the] camp of Aram to hear [the] sound of chariotry, [the] sound of horse, [the] sound of a great army; and they said each to his brother, Look, has hired against us [the] king of Israel the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to come against us.
pieces: The Lord had made the Aramean army hear the sound of chariots and horses, the sound of a great army, and they said to one another, "Look, the king of Israel has hired the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to attack us!"

L.6: For the Lord had made the camp of Aram hear a sound of chariots, a sound of horses, a sound of a great army, and they said each to his brother, "Look, the king of Israel has hired against us the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to come against us."

R.6: This was because the Lord had made the Aramean soldiers hear the sound of chariots and horses and a huge army. They said to each other, "The king of Israel has paid the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt to come and attack us!"

decisions.choice: the Lord had made them hear: what had already happened before the men arrived
decisions.reason: The sentence puts its subject first and breaks the chain of events. It goes back in time to explain why the camp was empty in verse 5.

decisions.choice: the Lord caused the sound: God's own doing, without a battle
decisions.reason: The verse calls God "the Lord" (the title Adonai) here, not by his name, and says plainly that the noise came from him. No army of Israel was there. Compare the horses and chariots of fire around Elisha (6:17) and the sound of marching in the treetops in 2 Samuel 5:24.

decisions.choice: the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Egypt: hired armies from north and south
alternatives: Musri, a land in the north
decisions.reason: Long after the Hittite empire ended, small kingdoms north of Aram, in northern Syria and southern Turkey, were still called Hittite (1 Kings 10:29). Egypt lay to the south. The Arameans feared being caught between two forces. Some suggest "Egypt" here is a similar name for a land in the north, but the text as it stands names Egypt.

decisions.choice: hired: paid foreign kings to fight
decisions.reason: Kings did hire other kings' armies (2 Samuel 10:6; 1 Kings 15:18-19). The Arameans think that Israel has done so.

decisions.choice: the Aramean army; the Aramean soldiers
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "the camp of Aram"; the word for camp also means the army in it, and that is who heard the sound.

records.source: וַיָּקוּמוּ֮ וַיָּנ֣וּסוּ בַנֶּשֶׁף֒ וַיַּעַזְב֣וּ אֶת־אָהֳלֵיהֶ֗ם וְאֶת־סֽוּסֵיהֶם֙ וְאֶת־חֲמֹ֣רֵיהֶ֔ם הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֖ה כַּאֲשֶׁר־הִ֑יא וַיָּנֻ֖סוּ אֶל־נַפְשָֽׁם׃
records.gloss: And they arose and fled at twilight and abandoned their tents and their horses and their donkeys, the camp as it [was], and fled for their life.
pieces: So they got up and ran away at dusk, abandoning their tents, their horses and their donkeys. They left the camp just as it was and ran for their lives.

L.7: And they got up and fled at twilight, and they abandoned their tents and their horses and their donkeys, the camp just as it [was], and they fled for their lives.

R.7: So that evening they got up and ran away. They left behind their tents, their horses and their donkeys. They left the whole camp just as it was and ran to save their lives.

decisions.choice: at twilight: the same evening the four men set out
decisions.reason: The word is the one in verse 5. The Arameans fled at dusk and the four men set out at dusk, so the camp had only just been emptied when they arrived.

decisions.choice: fled for their life: ran to save their lives
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says they fled "to their life", meaning to save it (compare 1 Kings 19:3).

decisions.choice: they left their horses and donkeys: they ran on foot
decisions.reason: The soldiers did not stop even to untie their animals (verse 10). Leaving them shows how great the panic was.

decisions.choice: that evening
decisions.reason: Readable says "that evening" for "at twilight", which also shows it was the same evening as verse 5.

records.source: וַיָּבֹאוּ֩ הַֽמְצֹרָעִ֨ים הָאֵ֜לֶּה עַד־קְצֵ֣ה הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֗ה וַיָּבֹ֜אוּ אֶל־אֹ֤הֶל אֶחָד֙ וַיֹּאכְל֣וּ וַיִּשְׁתּ֔וּ וַיִּשְׂא֣וּ מִשָּׁ֗ם כֶּ֤סֶף וְזָהָב֙ וּבְגָדִ֔ים וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ וַיַּטְמִ֑נוּ וַיָּשֻׁ֗בוּ וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ אֶל־אֹ֣הֶל אַחֵ֔ר וַיִּשְׂא֣וּ מִשָּׁ֔ם וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ וַיַּטְמִֽנוּ׃
records.gloss: And came these [men with] scale disease to [the] edge of the camp, and went into one tent and ate and drank, and carried from there silver and gold and clothes, and went and hid [them]; and returned and went into another tent and carried from there, and went and hid [them].
pieces: When these men with the skin disease reached the edge of the camp, they went into one tent and ate and drank. They carried off silver, gold and clothing from it and went and hid them. Then they came back, went into another tent, carried off things from there too, and went and hid them.

L.8: And these men with scale disease came to the edge of the camp, and they went into one tent and ate and drank, and carried off from there silver and gold and clothes, and went and hid [them]. And they came back and went into another tent and carried off [things] from there, and went and hid [them].

R.8: The four men came to the edge of the camp and went into one of the tents. They ate and drank. Then they took silver, gold and clothes from the tent and went and hid them. They came back, went into another tent, took more things, and hid those too.

decisions.choice: these men with scale disease: the four of verse 3
decisions.reason: The narrator now calls them by their disease, as in verse 3; it marks them as outsiders, the last people anyone would expect to find the camp.

decisions.choice: silver, gold and clothes: valuable plunder
decisions.reason: Fine clothing was wealth that could be stored and traded, alongside silver and gold (Joshua 7:21; 5:5 in this book). The men hide it to keep it before others come.

decisions.choice: went and hid them: the same action twice
decisions.reason: The repeated verbs show the men going back and forth, filling themselves and storing up wealth before they think of anyone else (verse 9).

decisions.choice: hid them; took more things
decisions.reason: The Hebrew leaves the objects of "hid" and the second "carried off" unstated. Balanced and Readable supply them, as Literal does in brackets. Readable says "the four men" for "these men with scale disease".

records.source: וַיֹּאמְרוּ֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֜הוּ לֹֽא־כֵ֣ן׀אֲנַ֣חְנוּ עֹשִׂ֗ים הַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ יוֹם־בְּשֹׂרָ֣ה ה֔וּא וַאֲנַ֣חְנוּ מַחְשִׁ֗ים וְחִכִּ֛ינוּ עַד־א֥וֹר הַבֹּ֖קֶר וּמְצָאָ֣נוּ עָו֑וֹן וְעַתָּה֙ לְכ֣וּ וְנָבֹ֔אָה וְנַגִּ֖ידָה בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And said each to his neighbor, Not right we [are] doing; this day, a day of good news it [is], and we [are] keeping silent; and [if] we wait until [the] light of the morning, and will find us punishment; and now come and let us go and tell [the] household of the king.
pieces: Then they said to one another, "What we are doing is not right. This is a day of good news, and we are keeping it to ourselves. If we wait until daylight, punishment will catch up with us. Come, let us go and report this to the king's household."

L.9: Then they said each to his companion, "We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news, and we are keeping silent. If we wait until the light of morning, guilt will find us. So now come, let us go and tell the household of the king."

R.9: Then they said to each other, "We are doing wrong. Today is a day of good news, and we are not telling anyone! If we wait until morning, we will be punished. Let us go right now and tell the people at the king's palace."

decisions.choice: good news: a report that brings relief, here the enemy's flight
decisions.reason: The word names good news carried to others, often news of victory (2 Samuel 18:20-27). The related verb is used for bringing good news of Yahweh's rescue (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7). The men see that such news is not theirs to keep.

decisions.choice: guilt will find us: we will be punished for our wrong
decisions.reason: The word means both a wrong and the punishment it brings. To be "found" by it is to have it catch up with you (compare Numbers 32:23). The men fear the king's anger if they are found to have hidden the news.

decisions.choice: if we wait ...: a condition without "if"
decisions.reason: Hebrew can join two clauses with "and" where the first states a condition and the second its result: "we wait ..., and punishment will find us".

decisions.choice: the king's household: the people of the palace
decisions.reason: The household is the king's palace and the officials in it, who could wake the king (verses 11-12).

decisions.choice: keeping it to ourselves; not telling anyone
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "we are keeping silent". Balanced and Readable say what the silence is: the news is not being passed on.

records.source: וַיָּבֹ֗אוּ וַֽיִּקְרְאוּ֮ אֶל־שֹׁעֵ֣ר הָעִיר֒ וַיַּגִּ֤ידוּ לָהֶם֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר בָּ֚אנוּ אֶל־מַחֲנֵ֣ה אֲרָ֔ם וְהִנֵּ֥ה אֵֽין־שָׁ֛ם אִ֖ישׁ וְק֣וֹל אָדָ֑ם כִּ֣י אִם־הַסּ֤וּס אָסוּר֙ וְהַחֲמ֣וֹר אָס֔וּר וְאֹהָלִ֖ים כַּאֲשֶׁר־הֵֽמָּה׃
records.gloss: And they came and called to [the] gatekeeper of the city and told them, saying, We went to [the] camp of Aram, and look, there was not there a man or [the] sound of a human, but only the horse tied and the donkey tied and tents as they [were].
pieces: So they came back and called out to the gatekeepers of the city and told them, "We went to the Aramean camp, and there was no one there, not a human voice to be heard. There were only horses tied up and donkeys tied up, and the tents left just as they were."

L.10: And they came and called to the gatekeeper of the city, and they told them, saying, "We went to the camp of Aram, and look, there was no one there, nor the voice of a human, but only the horses tied, and the donkeys tied, and the tents just as they [were]."

R.10: So they went back to the city and shouted to the men guarding the gate. They told them, "We went to the Aramean camp, and no one was there! We did not hear a single voice. The horses and donkeys were still tied up, and the tents were standing there just as the soldiers had left them."

decisions.choice: the gatekeeper ... told them: one word for the guards as a group
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "gatekeeper" but then "told them", and verse 11 speaks of "the gatekeepers". The singular stands for the guards of the city gate as a group.

decisions.choice: the voice of a human: any human sound
decisions.reason: The word for sound is the one used in verse 6. The Arameans heard the sound of a great army; the four men heard no human sound at all.

decisions.choice: the horse ... the donkey: horses and donkeys
decisions.reason: The singular with "the" names the animals as a kind, meaning all the horses and donkeys of the camp (verse 7).

decisions.choice: the gatekeepers; the men guarding the gate
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the plural, which the following "them" requires in English (m1).

decisions.choice: just as the soldiers had left them
decisions.reason: Readable says who left the tents.

records.source: וַיִּקְרָ֖א הַשֹּֽׁעֲרִ֑ים וַיַּגִּ֕ידוּ בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ פְּנִֽימָה׃
records.gloss: And called the gatekeepers, and they told [the] household of the king within.
pieces: The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported inside the king's palace.

L.11: And the gatekeepers called out, and they told [it to] the household of the king within.

R.11: The gatekeepers called out the news, and it was passed on to the people inside the king's palace.

decisions.choice: the gatekeepers called out, and they told: the news passed on from the gate
decisions.reason: The first verb is singular and the second plural; both have the gatekeepers as a group for their subject (compare verse 10). They shouted the news from the gate, and it was carried into the palace.

decisions.choice: the household of the king within: the people inside the palace
decisions.reason: "Within" points to the inner rooms of the palace, where the king was asleep (verse 12).

decisions.choice: it was reported; it was passed on
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn "they told the household" into a passive, since the point is that the news reached the palace, and add "the news" as what was shouted.

records.source: וַיָּ֨קָם הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לַ֗יְלָה וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־עֲבָדָ֔יו אַגִּֽידָה־נָּ֣א לָכֶ֔ם אֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁר־עָ֥שׂוּ לָ֖נוּ אֲרָ֑ם יָדְע֞וּ כִּי־רְעֵבִ֣ים אֲנַ֗חְנוּ וַיֵּצְא֤וּ מִן־הַֽמַּחֲנֶה֙ לְהֵחָבֵ֤ה בַשָּׂדֶה֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר כִּֽי־יֵצְא֤וּ מִן־הָעִיר֙ וְנִתְפְּשֵׂ֣ם חַיִּ֔ים וְאֶל־הָעִ֖יר נָבֹֽא׃
records.gloss: And arose the king [by] night and said to his servants, Let me tell you please what have done to us Aram; they know that hungry [are] we, and they went out from the camp to hide in the field, saying, When they come out from the city, and we will seize them alive, and into the city we will go.
pieces: The king got up in the night and said to his officials, "I will explain to you what the Arameans have done to us. They know that we are starving, and they have left their camp to hide out in the countryside. They are thinking, 'When they come out of the city, we will capture them alive and get into the city.'"

L.12: And the king got up in the night and said to his servants, "Let me tell you what Aram has done to us. They know that we are hungry, and they have gone out of the camp to hide in the field, saying, 'When they come out of the city, we will seize them alive and get into the city.'"

R.12: The king got up in the middle of the night. He said to his officials, "I know what the Arameans are doing to us. They know that we are starving. So they have left their camp and are hiding out in the fields. They think, 'When the people come out of the city, we will catch them alive. Then we can get into the city.'"

decisions.choice: they have gone out to hide in the field: the king suspects an ambush
decisions.reason: Pretending to retreat and then cutting off those who follow was a known trick of war; Joshua used it at Ai (Joshua 8:4-22). The king, who did not believe Elisha (6:31-33), assumes a trap.

decisions.choice: in the field: written with "the", read without it
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has the article ("in the field"), and the marginal reading of the Masoretes reads the word without it. The sense is the same: the open country outside the city.

decisions.choice: saying: thinking to themselves
decisions.reason: The word that usually introduces speech here gives the plan the king imagines the Arameans have made.

decisions.choice: hungry: starving
decisions.reason: The word means hungry, but in a city where people had eaten their own children (6:28-29) it means starving.

decisions.choice: his officials
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "his servants" (Literal). Here they are the king's court officials, so Balanced and Readable say "officials", as elsewhere in Kings.

decisions.choice: I know what the Arameans are doing to us; when the people come out
decisions.reason: Readable turns "let me tell you" into a plain statement and says who would come out of the city.

records.source: וַיַּעַן֩ אֶחָ֨ד מֵעֲבָדָ֜יו וַיֹּ֗אמֶר וְיִקְחוּ־נָ֞א חֲמִשָּׁ֣ה מִן־הַסּוּסִים֮ הַֽנִּשְׁאָרִים֮ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִשְׁאֲרוּ־בָהּ֒ הִנָּ֗ם כְּכָל־הֲמ֤וֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִשְׁאֲרוּ־בָ֔הּ הִנָּ֕ם כְּכָל־הֲמ֥וֹן יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁר־תָּ֑מּוּ וְנִשְׁלְחָ֖ה וְנִרְאֶֽה׃
records.gloss: And answered one of his servants and said, And let them take please five of the horses that remain, which are left in it; look, they [are] like all [the] multitude of Israel that are left in it; look, they [are] like all [the] multitude of Israel that have come to an end; and let us send and let us see.
pieces: One of his officials answered, "Have some men take five of the horses still left in the city. Whatever happens to them, they are only like the rest of the people of Israel who are left here, like all the people of Israel who have already perished. Let us send them and see."

L.13: And one of his servants answered and said, "Let [men] take, please, five of the remaining horses that are left in it. Look, they [are] like all the multitude of Israel who are left in it; look, they [are] like all the multitude of Israel who have come to an end. And let us send and see."

R.13: One of his officials answered, "Let some men take five of the horses that are still left in the city. If they stay here, they will end up like everyone else in Israel who has already died. So let us send them out and see what has happened."

decisions.choice: the comparison given twice
decisions.reason: The standard Hebrew text says "they are like all the multitude of Israel" twice, first of those who are left, then of those who have perished; in the first, the written text also has an extra "the" that is not read. Some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient translations have the comparison only once, which may be the result of a copyist's eye skipping. This translation follows the standard text, but the sense is much the same either way.

decisions.choice: they are like the rest of Israel: sending the horses risks little
decisions.reason: The horses still alive will share the fate of the city: they are left for now, like the people left in Samaria, but they will die as so many others have died. So it costs little to risk them on a scouting trip.

decisions.choice: in it: in the city
decisions.reason: "It" is feminine in Hebrew and refers to the city, Samaria.

decisions.choice: have come to an end: have perished
decisions.reason: The verb means to be finished or used up; of people it means to die off (Numbers 14:35; Deuteronomy 2:16).

decisions.choice: his officials
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "his servants" (Literal). Here they are the king's court officials, so Balanced and Readable say "officials", as elsewhere in Kings.

decisions.choice: Whatever happens to them, they are only like ...; If they stay here, they will end up like ...
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add a few words to make the official's reasoning clear (m2). Readable keeps only the second comparison, which carries the point.

records.source: וַיִּקְח֕וּ שְׁנֵ֖י רֶ֣כֶב סוּסִ֑ים וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ אַחֲרֵ֧י מַחֲנֵֽה־אֲרָ֛ם לֵאמֹ֖ר לְכ֥וּ וּרְאֽוּ׃
records.gloss: And they took two chariot[s of] horses, and sent the king after [the] camp of Aram, saying, Go and see.
pieces: So they took two chariots with their horses, and the king sent them after the Aramean army with the order, "Go and find out."

L.14: So they took two chariots [with] horses, and the king sent [them] after the camp of Aram, saying, "Go and see."

R.14: So they got two chariots with horses, and the king sent them to follow the Aramean army. He told the men, "Go and find out what has happened."

decisions.choice: two chariots with horses: two chariot teams
decisions.reason: The phrase is short: literally "two chariot horses". It most likely means two chariots with their teams, which fits the five horses offered in verse 13 (two pairs and a spare). It could also mean two pairs of chariot horses ridden by scouts.

decisions.choice: the camp of Aram: here, the army on the move
decisions.reason: The word for camp also names the army that camps in it. The scouts follow the army, not the empty camp.

decisions.choice: find out what has happened
decisions.reason: Readable says what the scouts were to see.

records.source: וַיֵּלְכ֣וּ אַחֲרֵיהֶם֮ עַד־הַיַּרְדֵּן֒ וְהִנֵּ֣ה כָל־הַדֶּ֗רֶךְ מְלֵאָ֤ה בְגָדִים֙ וְכֵלִ֔ים אֲשֶׁר־הִשְׁלִ֥יכוּ אֲרָ֖ם בְּחָפְזָ֑ם וַיָּשֻׁ֨בוּ֙ הַמַּלְאָכִ֔ים וַיַּגִּ֖דוּ לַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And they went after them to the Jordan, and look, all the way [was] full [of] clothes and equipment which had thrown Aram in their haste; and returned the messengers and told the king.
pieces: They followed them as far as the Jordan, and the whole road was strewn with clothing and gear that the Arameans had flung away as they fled in haste. The messengers came back and reported to the king.

L.15: And they went after them as far as the Jordan, and look, all the way [was] full of clothes and equipment that Aram had thrown away in their haste. And the messengers returned and told the king.

R.15: They followed the Arameans all the way to the Jordan River. The whole road was covered with clothes and equipment that the Arameans had thrown away as they ran. The men came back and told the king.

decisions.choice: as far as the Jordan: a long way east
decisions.reason: The Arameans were heading home to Damascus, which meant crossing the Jordan valley. The river lay some 25 miles east of Samaria, so the scouts followed a long way.

decisions.choice: in their haste: two forms of the same word
decisions.reason: The written text has one form of the verb "hurry" and the Masoretes' marginal reading another. Both mean "as they hurried".

decisions.choice: equipment: gear of any kind
decisions.reason: The word covers containers, tools and weapons. Fleeing soldiers threw away whatever slowed them down.

decisions.choice: the Arameans
decisions.reason: As through the chapter, Balanced and Readable say "the Arameans" for "Aram". Readable says "the men" for "the messengers".

records.source: וַיֵּצֵ֣א הָעָ֔ם וַיָּבֹ֕זּוּ אֵ֖ת מַחֲנֵ֣ה אֲרָ֑ם וַיְהִ֨י סְאָה־סֹ֜לֶת בְּשֶׁ֗קֶל וְסָאתַ֧יִם שְׂעֹרִ֛ים בְּשֶׁ֖קֶל כִּדְבַ֥ר יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And went out the people and plundered [the] camp of Aram; and was a seah of fine flour for a shekel and two seahs of barley for a shekel, according to [the] word of Yahweh.
pieces: Then the people went out and plundered the Aramean camp. So {{units:about 7 quarts|a seah}} of fine flour sold for {{units:about 2/5 ounce of silver|a shekel}}, and {{units:about 13 quarts|two seahs}} of barley for {{units:about 2/5 ounce of silver|a shekel}}, just as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had said.

L.16: And the people went out and plundered the camp of Aram, and a seah of fine flour [sold] for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, according to the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.16: Then the people of the city went out and took everything they wanted from the Aramean camp. So {{units:about 7 quarts|a seah}} of the best flour sold for {{units:about 2/5 ounce of silver|a shekel}}, and {{units:about 13 quarts|two seahs}} of barley sold for the same price. It happened just as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had said it would.

decisions.choice: according to the word of Yahweh: Elisha's word came true
decisions.reason: The prices are word for word those of verse 1. The narrator stresses that the word came from Yahweh and that it was fulfilled exactly, within the day.

decisions.choice: the people: the people of Samaria
decisions.reason: Here the people are the starving citizens, not an army. They poured out of the gate to the camp.

decisions.choice: a seah ... a shekel: as in verse 1
decisions.reason: As in verse 1.

decisions.choice: about 7 quarts; about 13 quarts; about 2/5 ounce of silver
decisions.reason: As in verse 1. Readable says "the same price" for the second shekel and adds "of the city".

records.source: וְהַמֶּלֶךְ֩ הִפְקִ֨יד אֶת־הַשָּׁלִ֜ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־נִשְׁעָ֤ן עַל־יָדוֹ֙ עַל־הַשַּׁ֔עַר וַיִּרְמְסֻ֧הוּ הָעָ֛ם בַּשַּׁ֖עַר וַיָּמֹ֑ת כַּאֲשֶׁ֤ר דִּבֶּר֙ אִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר דִּבֶּ֔ר בְּרֶ֥דֶת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֵלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And the king had appointed the officer on whose hand he leaned over the gate; and trampled him the people in the gate, and he died, as had spoken [the] man of God, who spoke when came down the king to him.
pieces: Now the king had put the officer on whose arm he leaned in charge of the gate. In the gateway the people trampled him, and he died, as the man of God had foretold when the king came down to him.

L.17: Now the king had appointed the officer on whose hand he leaned over the gate, and the people trampled him in the gate, and he died, just as the man of God had spoken, which he spoke when the king came down to him.

R.17: The king had put his personal officer, the man he leaned on, in charge of the city gate. But the crowd of people ran over him in the gateway, and he died. It happened just as the man of God had said when the king came down to see him.

decisions.choice: the king had appointed: background to the officer's death
decisions.reason: The sentence puts "the king" first and steps out of the chain of events, explaining why the officer was at the gate when the crowd rushed out.

decisions.choice: trampled him in the gate: crushed by the crowd
decisions.reason: The officer was set to keep order at the gate, the only way out to the camp and the place where food was now sold (verse 1). The starving crowd pushed through and trampled him.

decisions.choice: when the king came down to him: the scene of 6:32-33
decisions.reason: This refers to the king's coming to Elisha's house after his messenger (6:32-33), where Elisha spoke the word of verse 1. Verse 2 shows that the king's officer was there with him.

decisions.choice: and he died, as the man of God had said: the second half of the word fulfilled
decisions.reason: Elisha had told the officer that he would see the plenty but not eat of it (verse 2). Verses 18-20 repeat the exchange to show that both halves came true.

decisions.choice: the crowd of people ran over him
decisions.reason: Readable says "crowd" and "ran over" to make the picture of the rush clear.

records.source: וַיְהִ֗י כְּדַבֵּר֙ אִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים אֶל־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לֵאמֹ֑ר סָאתַ֨יִם שְׂעֹרִ֜ים בְּשֶׁ֗קֶל וּֽסְאָה־סֹ֨לֶת֙ בְּשֶׁ֔קֶל יִהְיֶה֙ כָּעֵ֣ת מָחָ֔ר בְּשַׁ֖עַר שֹׁמְרֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And it was, when spoke the man of God to the king, saying, Two seahs of barley for a shekel and a seah of fine flour for a shekel will be about [this] time tomorrow in [the] gate of Samaria,
pieces: For when the man of God told the king, "{{units:About 13 quarts|Two seahs}} of barley will sell for {{units:about 2/5 ounce of silver|a shekel}}, and {{units:about 7 quarts|a seah}} of fine flour for {{units:about 2/5 ounce of silver|a shekel}}, about this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria,"

L.18: And it was, when the man of God spoke to the king, saying, "Two seahs of barley for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour for a shekel, will be [sold] about [this] time tomorrow in the gate of Samaria,"

R.18: The man of God had told the king, "By this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, you will be able to buy {{units:about 13 quarts|two seahs}} of barley for {{units:about 2/5 ounce of silver|a shekel}}, or {{units:about 7 quarts|a seah}} of the best flour for the same price."

decisions.choice: the word of verse 1 repeated
decisions.reason: The narrator repeats Elisha's word from verse 1, now naming barley first. The repetition stresses that what happened was exactly what had been foretold.

decisions.choice: and it was, when ...: a sentence that continues into verse 19
decisions.reason: This verse sets the time, and the main clause comes in verse 19: "the officer answered". The two verses go back to verse 2.

decisions.choice: about 13 quarts; about 7 quarts; about 2/5 ounce of silver
decisions.reason: As in verse 1. Readable ends the sentence here and lets verse 19 begin a new one.

records.source: וַיַּ֨עַן הַשָּׁלִ֜ישׁ אֶת־אִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים֮ וַיֹּאמַר֒ וְהִנֵּ֣ה יְהוָ֗ה עֹשֶׂ֤ה אֲרֻבּוֹת֙ בַּשָּׁמַ֔יִם הֲיִהְיֶ֖ה כַּדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הִנְּךָ֤ רֹאֶה֙ בְּעֵינֶ֔יךָ וּמִשָּׁ֖ם לֹ֥א תֹאכֵֽל׃
records.gloss: and answered the officer the man of God and said, And look, Yahweh [is] making windows in the heavens; will [it] be according to this thing? And he said, Look, you [are] seeing with your eyes, but from there not you will eat.
pieces: the officer had answered the man of God, "Even if {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} were to make floodgates in the heavens, could such a thing happen?" And Elisha had replied, "With your own eyes you will see it happen, but you will not eat any of it."

L.19: then the officer answered the man of God and said, "Now look, [even if] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} were making windows in the heavens, could it be according to this word?" And he said, "Look, you are going to see [it] with your own eyes, but you will not eat from it."

R.19: The officer had answered, "Even if {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} opened windows in the sky, could this really happen?" And the man of God had said, "You will see it happen with your own eyes. But you will not eat any of that food."

decisions.choice: the exchange of verse 2 repeated
decisions.reason: The officer's words and Elisha's reply repeat verse 2 almost word for word. The officer's question here reads "could it be according to this word?" where verse 2 has "could this word happen?"; the sense is the same.

decisions.choice: look, if Yahweh made windows ...: a scornful "even if"
decisions.reason: As in verse 2: the question expects the answer no.

decisions.choice: windows in the heavens: as in verse 2
decisions.reason: As in verse 2 (Genesis 7:11).

decisions.choice: had answered; had replied
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use "had" because these words were spoken the day before, as verse 18 tells. Balanced uses "floodgates" as in verse 2.

records.source: וַיְהִי־ל֖וֹ כֵּ֑ן וַיִּרְמְס֨וּ אֹת֥וֹ הָעָ֛ם בַּשַּׁ֖עַר וַיָּמֹֽת׃ס
records.gloss: And it happened to him so; and trampled him the people in the gate, and he died.
pieces: And that is exactly how it ended for him: in the gateway the people trampled him, and he died.

L.20: And so it happened to him: the people trampled him in the gate, and he died.

R.20: That is just what happened to him. The crowd at the city gate trampled him, and he died.

decisions.choice: so it happened to him: the prophet's word came true
decisions.reason: The chapter ends by repeating the end of verse 17. The man who mocked the word of Yahweh saw the plenty but did not live to eat it.

decisions.choice: and the people trampled him: how it happened
decisions.reason: The second clause explains the first: what happened to him was that he was trampled.

decisions.choice: exactly; just
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "exactly" or "just" to carry the force of "so", which points back to Elisha's word.
